<!-- ## Package sf -->

<!-- `sf` implements the OGC *Simple Features* standard in R. An `sf` object is a `data.frame` (or tibble) with a **geometry list-column** of class `sfc`, whose elements are individual geometries of class `sfg`. Three classes, nested: -->

<!-- - `sfg` — one geometry: a point, a line, a polygon -->
<!-- - `sfc` — a column of geometries, with a CRS and a bounding box -->
<!-- - `sf` — a data frame with an `sfc` column and attribute columns -->

<!-- Functions and methods for these objects start with `st_` (for *spatial and temporal*), which makes them easy to find with tab completion. -->

<!-- An `sf` object carries the name of its active geometry column (attribute `sf_column`) and, for each attribute, an attribute–geometry relationship (`agr`: constant, aggregate or identity). An `sfc` column carries `crs`, `bbox`, `precision` and `n_empty`. Get and set these with `st_crs()`, `st_bbox()`, `st_agr()`, `st_precision()` and their `st_set_*` versions. -->

<!-- ### Creation -->

<!-- Most spatial data are read from somewhere, but building an object by hand shows you what the pieces are. Three hypothetical stream-temperature loggers in the watershed, given as longitude/latitude: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: create -->
<!-- p1 <- st_point(c(-123.30, 53.75)) -->
<!-- p2 <- st_point(c(-123.65, 53.55)) -->
<!-- p3 <- st_point(c(-123.95, 53.40)) -->
<!-- class(p1) -->

<!-- sfc <- st_sfc(list(p1, p2, p3), crs = "OGC:CRS84") -->
<!-- class(sfc) -->
<!-- st_crs(sfc)$input -->

<!-- loggers <- st_sf(site = c("CHK-01", "CHK-02", "CHK-03"), -->
<!--                  elev_m = c(720, 860, 1010), -->
<!--                  geom = sfc) -->
<!-- loggers -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- The coordinates are illustrative. Section 5.2 checks whether they actually fall inside the watershed; if one doesn't, move it — that is exactly the kind of check you should run on any coordinates someone hands you. -->

<!-- Read the header: three features, two fields, geometry type `POINT`, dimension `XY`, a bounding box, and a geodetic CRS. `OGC:CRS84` is WGS 84 with axes in longitude–latitude order; it avoids the axis-order ambiguity of `EPSG:4326` (see @sec-axis). -->

<!-- ### Reading and writing -->

<!-- `st_read()` takes a *data source name* (`dsn`) and a *layer*. A GeoPackage can hold many layers; list them first. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: layers -->
<!-- gpkg <- "data/chilako.gpkg" -->
<!-- st_layers(gpkg) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: read -->
<!-- ws        <- st_read(gpkg, layer = "watershed", quiet = TRUE) -->
<!-- streams   <- st_read(gpkg, layer = "streams",   quiet = TRUE) -->
<!-- lakes     <- st_read(gpkg, layer = "lakes",     quiet = TRUE) -->
<!-- cutblocks <- st_read(gpkg, layer = "cutblocks", quiet = TRUE) -->
<!-- fires     <- st_read(gpkg, layer = "fires",     quiet = TRUE) -->

<!-- ws -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- If you omit `layer` on a multi-layer file, `st_read()` reads the first layer and warns. Get in the habit of naming it. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: overview-map -->
<!-- #| fig-height: 7 -->
<!-- ggplot() + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = ws, fill = "grey95") + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = cutblocks, fill = "darkseagreen", colour = NA) + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = fires, fill = "orange", alpha = 0.5, colour = NA) + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = lakes, fill = "steelblue", colour = NA) + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = streams, colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.3) + -->
<!--   theme_minimal() -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- Writing uses `st_write()`; the format comes from the file extension. Write the loggers into the same GeoPackage as a new layer: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: write -->
<!-- #| cache: false -->
<!-- st_write(loggers, gpkg, layer = "loggers", delete_layer = TRUE, quiet = TRUE) -->
<!-- st_layers(gpkg)$name -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- `st_write()` errors if the layer already exists unless you tell it what to do: `append = TRUE` adds records, `delete_layer = TRUE` replaces the layer, `delete_dsn = TRUE` deletes the whole file first. The tidyverse-style `write_sf()` replaces silently. `st_delete()` removes a layer, useful when the "layer" is a table in a database. -->

<!-- The GeoPackage stores the CRS as WKT-2, so it comes back intact. A CSV cannot store a CRS at all; a shapefile stores a lossy approximation. That is the practical reason to prefer GeoPackage. -->

<!-- ::: callout-tip -->
<!-- ## Two errors you will meet with `st_write()` -->

<!-- *"database is locked"* — another program (QGIS, ArcGIS Pro, another R session) has the GeoPackage open. Close it. -->

<!-- *"duplicate names present"* — two columns differ only in case (`AREA_HA` and `area_ha`). GeoPackage field names are case-insensitive. Rename one. -->
<!-- ::: -->

<!-- ### Subsetting -->

<!-- Base `[` works on an `sf` object the way it works on a data frame, with two additions. First, the geometry column is *always* kept unless you say `drop = TRUE` and leave it out of the selection: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: subset -->
<!-- cutblocks[1:3, "HARVEST_YEAR"] -->
<!-- cutblocks[1:3, "HARVEST_YEAR", drop = TRUE] -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- Second, if the first index is itself a spatial object, the rows selected are the features that spatially **intersect** it. Cutblocks that touch the largest fire in the record: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: spatial-subset -->
<!-- big_fire <- fires |> mutate(area = st_area(geom)) |> slice_max(area, n = 1) -->
<!-- cutblocks[big_fire, ] -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- A different predicate goes in `op`: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: spatial-subset-op -->
<!-- cutblocks[big_fire, , op = st_within] |> nrow()   # entirely inside the perimeter -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- Any binary predicate from the next section can be used. -->

<!-- ### Binary predicates -->

<!-- `st_intersects()`, `st_within()`, `st_touches()` and the rest take two sets of geometries and answer, for every pair, TRUE or FALSE. For large sets that matrix would be enormous and almost all FALSE, so by default a **sparse** representation is returned: a list with one element per row of `x`, holding the column indices of `y` that are TRUE. -->

<!-- Which named lakes do the first ten stream segments intersect? -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: sgbp -->
<!-- s10 <- streams[1:10, ] -->
<!-- (i <- st_intersects(s10, lakes)) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- The object is of class `sgbp` (sparse geometrical binary predicate). Turn it into a dense matrix, or count matches per row or per column: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: sgbp-2 -->
<!-- dim(as.matrix(i)) -->
<!-- lengths(i)        # lakes intersected by each of the 10 segments -->
<!-- sum(lengths(i) > 0) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- `t()` flips it so you can count the other way — for every lake, how many of these segments touch it: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: sgbp-3 -->
<!-- table(lengths(t(i))) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- The only arithmetic method for `sgbp` is `!`, negation. `st_disjoint()` is `!st_intersects()`. -->

<!-- A predicate that takes a distance, `st_is_within_distance()`, needs a unit because our CRS is in metres: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: within-distance -->
<!-- near <- st_is_within_distance(big_fire, lakes, set_units(200, m)) -->
<!-- sum(lengths(near) > 0)   # cutblocks within 200 m of any lake -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- ### tidyverse -->

<!-- `sf` provides methods so that the dplyr verbs work on `sf` objects and the geometry column survives: `filter`, `select`, `mutate`, `group_by`, `summarise`, `slice`, `distinct`, `rename`, `arrange` and more. `read_sf()` and `write_sf()` are the tidyverse-style read/write: tibbles, no printing, overwrite by default. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: read-sf -->
<!-- cutblocks <- read_sf(gpkg, layer = "cutblocks") -->
<!-- class(cutblocks) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- `select()` keeps the geometry. When you want a plain table, drop it explicitly: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: tidy-select -->
<!-- cutblocks |> select(HARVEST_YEAR) |> head(3) -->
<!-- cutblocks |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(HARVEST_YEAR) |> head(3) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- `summarise()` on an `sf` object has two extra arguments. `do_union` (default `TRUE`) unions the geometries of each group, so that a group's geometry is a single valid (multi)polygon — this is a dissolve. `is_coverage = TRUE` speeds the union when the inputs don't overlap. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: dissolve -->
<!-- cb_decade <- cutblocks |> -->
<!--   mutate(decade = floor(HARVEST_YEAR / 10) * 10) |> -->
<!--   group_by(decade) |> -->
<!--   summarise(n_blocks = n()) |> -->
<!--   mutate(area_ha = set_units(st_area(geom), ha)) -->

<!-- cb_decade |> st_drop_geometry() -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- Compare `sum(cb_decade$area_ha)` with `sum(st_area(cutblocks))`: the difference is the overlap between blocks (re-entry, salvage). Summing polygon areas double-counts; dissolve first when you want *ground area disturbed*. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: dissolve-map -->
<!-- ggplot() + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = ws, fill = "grey95") + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = cb_decade, aes(fill = factor(decade)), colour = NA) + -->
<!--   scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Decade") + -->
<!--   theme_minimal() -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- `distinct()` uses `st_equals()` to judge whether two geometries are the same. -->

<!-- `filter()` takes ordinary logical conditions. To filter on a *spatial* condition, compute the predicate first and filter on `lengths()`. Cutblocks within 2 km of a logger, following the book's Orange County example: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: filter-spatial -->
<!-- loggers_bca <- st_transform(loggers, st_crs(cutblocks)) -->
<!-- wd <- st_is_within_distance(cutblocks, loggers_bca, set_units(2, km)) -->
<!-- cb_near <- cutblocks |> dplyr::filter(lengths(wd) > 0) -->
<!-- nrow(cb_near) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: filter-spatial-map -->
<!-- #| code-fold: true -->
<!-- buf2k <- st_buffer(st_geometry(loggers_bca), set_units(2, km)) -->
<!-- ggplot() + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = ws, fill = "grey95") + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = cb_near, fill = "darkseagreen4", colour = NA) + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = buf2k, fill = NA, colour = "brown") + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = loggers_bca, colour = "brown", size = 2) + -->
<!--   theme_minimal() -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- The buffer is drawn for illustration; it was not used for the selection. `st_is_within_distance()` is both faster and exact. -->

<!-- ## Spatial joins -->

<!-- An attribute join matches records where a key is *equal*. A spatial join matches records where a *predicate is true*. Left/right/inner/full mean the same thing as in a database: what to do with records that have no match. -->

<!-- Attach the name of the stream that each cutblock touches: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: st-join -->
<!-- cb_streams <- st_join(cutblocks, streams["GNIS_NAME"], join = st_intersects) -->
<!-- nrow(cutblocks); nrow(cb_streams) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- The row count went up. A block crossed by three streams is now three rows, one per match — a spatial join is one-to-many. Two ways to bring it back to one row per feature: -->

<!-- **Keep the largest overlap.** Useful for polygon-on-polygon joins where each feature should get exactly one label. Build a 5 km grid over the watershed and label every cutblock with the cell it mostly lies in: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: largest -->
<!-- grid <- st_make_grid(ws, cellsize = 5000) |> -->
<!--   st_as_sf() |> -->
<!--   mutate(cell = row_number()) |> -->
<!--   st_filter(ws) -->

<!-- cb_cell <- st_join(cutblocks, grid, largest = TRUE) -->
<!-- nrow(cb_cell)              # one row per cutblock again -->
<!-- head(cb_cell$cell) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- **Aggregate after the join.** Total harvested area per grid cell, unioned so overlaps don't inflate it: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: aggregate -->
<!-- cb_by_cell <- cb_cell |> -->
<!--   group_by(cell) |> -->
<!--   summarise() |> -->
<!--   mutate(harvest_ha = set_units(st_area(geom), ha)) -->

<!-- ggplot() + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = grid, fill = NA, colour = "grey70") + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = cb_by_cell, aes(fill = as.numeric(harvest_ha)), colour = NA) + -->
<!--   scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Harvest (ha)") + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = ws, fill = NA) + -->
<!--   theme_minimal() -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- Base R's `aggregate()` does the same thing in one call: `aggregate(cutblocks["HARVEST_YEAR"], grid, length)` counts blocks per cell. -->

<!-- ### Sampling, gridding, interpolating -->

<!-- `st_sample()` draws points from point, line or polygon geometries — random, regular or hexagonal. Twenty random candidate sites on streams of order 5 and up: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: sample -->
<!-- set.seed(413) -->
<!-- mainstem <- streams |> filter(STREAM_ORDER >= 5) -->
<!-- cand <- st_sample(mainstem, 20) -->
<!-- length(cand) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- `st_make_grid()` you have seen; it also makes hexagons (`square = FALSE`) and grid centres or corners (`what = "centers"`). -->

<!-- `st_interpolate_aw()` does **area-weighted interpolation**: it moves attribute values from one set of polygons to another, proportional to the area of overlap. It needs to know whether the variable is *extensive* (a total, like area burned, which splits between target polygons) or *intensive* (a density or mean, which doesn't). Fire area is extensive. Move it from fire perimeters to the grid: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: aw -->
<!-- fires_u <- fires |> -->
<!--   group_by(FIRE_NUMBER) |> -->
<!--   summarise() |> -->
<!--   mutate(burn_ha = as.numeric(set_units(st_area(geom), ha))) -->

<!-- burn_grid <- st_interpolate_aw(fires_u["burn_ha"], grid, extensive = TRUE) -->

<!-- sum(burn_grid$burn_ha) -->
<!-- sum(fires_u$burn_ha) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- The totals match because an extensive variable is conserved. Dasymetric mapping is the same operation with an external weighting layer (`weights =`), for example redistributing a county population using a raster of dwellings. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: aw-map -->
<!-- #| code-fold: true -->
<!-- ggplot() + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = ws, fill = "grey95") + -->
<!--   geom_sf(data = burn_grid, aes(fill = burn_ha), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) + -->
<!--   scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Burned (ha)", option = "inferno", direction = -1) + -->
<!--   theme_minimal() -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- ## Ellipsoidal coordinates -->

<!-- Data in degrees are on an ellipsoid, not a plane. Since version 1.0, `sf` sends geodetic data to the **s2geometry** library, which treats a "straight" line as a great-circle arc. Projected data go to **GEOS**, which treats coordinates as Cartesian. -->

<!-- The consequence is easy to see on a big polygon. Take the watershed to WGS 84 and ask for its area both ways: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: s2 -->
<!-- ws_ll <- st_transform(ws, "OGC:CRS84") -->

<!-- st_area(ws_ll) |> set_units(km^2)            # s2: on the sphere -->

<!-- old <- sf_use_s2(FALSE) -->
<!-- st_area(ws_ll) |> set_units(km^2)            # GEOS: planar, degrees treated as metres — nonsense -->
<!-- sf_use_s2(old) -->

<!-- st_area(ws) |> set_units(km^2)               # BC Albers: the answer -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- Turning s2 off is occasionally useful — for speed, for compatibility with old code, or for `st_relate()` which only GEOS provides — but the safe default for analysis in BC is simpler: **transform to EPSG:3005 and let GEOS work in metres**. Note that the two libraries also differ in ring direction: GEOS returns exterior rings clockwise, s2 counter-clockwise; `st_sfc(..., check_ring_dir = TRUE)` normalises. -->

<!-- ## Coordinate transformations and conversions -->

<!-- ### `st_crs` -->

<!-- `st_crs()` gets or sets the CRS; `st_set_crs()` does the same in a pipe. It accepts an EPSG code, an `AUTHORITY:CODE` string, a name, a PROJ string, WKT-2 or PROJJSON. What it stores is WKT-2: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: crs -->
<!-- x <- st_crs(3005) -->
<!-- x$input -->
<!-- x$Name -->
<!-- cat(substr(x$wkt, 1, 300), "...") -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- A PROJ string can *define* a CRS but cannot fully *represent* one; `x$proj4string` will usually give you something, but the conversion is lossy and not always invertible. Don't pass PROJ strings around as a substitute for an EPSG code. -->

<!-- `st_crs()` only labels data. It never changes coordinates. If a layer arrives with no CRS and you know what it is, `st_set_crs()` is correct; if it arrives in the wrong CRS, `st_set_crs()` is a lie and `st_transform()` is what you want. -->

<!-- ### `st_transform`, `sf_project` -->

<!-- `st_transform()` converts coordinates between reference systems, choosing the most accurate operation PROJ knows about. Bring the loggers into BC Albers so they can be used with everything else: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: transform -->
<!-- loggers_bca <- st_transform(loggers, 3005) -->
<!-- st_crs(loggers_bca) == st_crs(ws) -->
<!-- nrow(loggers_bca[ws, ])  # how many of the three fall inside the watershed? -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- `sf_project()` is the low-level version for a bare coordinate matrix: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: sf-project -->
<!-- sf_project("OGC:CRS84", "EPSG:3005", st_coordinates(loggers)) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- ### `sf_proj_info` -->

<!-- Lists what PROJ has available: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: proj-info -->
<!-- sf_proj_info("proj") |> filter(name == "aea") -->
<!-- sf_proj_info("ellps") |> filter(name == "GRS80") -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- ### Datum grids, proj.db, the PROJ CDN -->

<!-- Transformations between datums (NAD27 → NAD83 → NAD83(CSRS)) can need grid files. PROJ looks for them on its search path; if absent and network access is on, it fetches the needed portion from <https://cdn.proj.org> and caches it locally. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: proj-db -->
<!-- sf_extSoftVersion()["PROJ"] -->
<!-- sf_proj_network() -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- BC's older paper mapping and much legacy digital data are NAD27. Transforming them without the datum grid silently gives a "ballpark" result of tens of metres. Check what you're getting. -->

<!-- ### Transformation pipelines -->

<!-- More than one route can exist from a source CRS to a target CRS. `sf_proj_pipelines()` lists them with declared accuracy; `st_transform()` picks the best available. NAD27 UTM zone 10 to BC Albers: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: pipelines -->
<!-- p <- sf_proj_pipelines("EPSG:26710", "EPSG:3005") -->
<!-- nrow(p) -->
<!-- p |> as.data.frame() |> select(accuracy, grid_count, definition) |> head(3) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- An `NA` accuracy means ballpark. If the most accurate pipeline needs a grid you don't have, you get the next one down — quietly. The `pipeline` argument to `st_transform()` lets you force a specific one. -->

<!-- ### Axis order and direction {#sec-axis} -->

<!-- The EPSG authority defines `EPSG:4326` with **latitude first**. Almost all software, and almost all files, store longitude first. `sf` follows practice, not the authority, by default; `st_axis_order(TRUE)` switches to authority order for the rare data source (some WFS servers) that is compliant. Using `OGC:CRS84` instead of `EPSG:4326` sidesteps the question: it is the same datum, explicitly longitude–latitude. -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| label: axes -->
<!-- st_crs("EPSG:4326")$axes -->
<!-- st_crs("OGC:CRS84")$axes -->
<!-- st_crs(3005)$axes -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- Not every CRS has axes pointing east and north; some southern-hemisphere and engineering systems don't, and most R plotting assumes they do. -->
